80262.q: How much Moon rock did all the Apollo flights bring back to Earth together?
80262.e: Together, the six Apollo landings brought back around 382 kilograms of stones and dust from the Moon.
80262.m: The Apollo astronauts brought back around 380 kilograms of Moon rock.

80263.q: What colour is most Moon rock?
80263.e: Moon rock is mostly light grey to dark grey. Moon dust is grey too.

80264.q: According to the astronauts, what did Moon dust smell like?
80264.e: When the astronauts took off their helmets after going outside, they smelt the dust in the lunar module. Many said it smelt like spent gunpowder.
80264.m: Moon dust smells like burnt gunpowder.

80265.q: How does Moon rock sometimes reach the Earth without any rocket?
80265.e: When a big chunk crashes into the Moon, stones can be thrown out into space. Some of them later fall onto the Earth as meteorites.
80265.m: Some meteorites are stones from the Moon.

80266.q: Which country brought Moon rock back to Earth with a space probe in 2020?
80266.e: The Chinese space probe Chang'e 5 landed on the Moon in 2020. It collected samples and brought them back to Earth with no people on board.
80266.m: In 2020 China collected Moon rock with a probe.

80267.q: Are there fossils of animals in Moon rock?
80267.e: There was never any life on the Moon. That is why there are no fossils in Moon rock either.
80267.m: There are no fossils in Moon rock.

80268.q: What is the dark rock of the lunar seas called?
80268.e: Basalt is a dark, hard rock. There is basalt on Earth too, for example near volcanoes.
80268.m: The dark seas on the Moon are made of basalt.

80269.q: Why did Moon dust stick so strongly to the spacesuits?
80269.e: On the Moon there is no water and no wind to wear the dust grains smooth. The sharp grains hooked onto everything.
80269.m: Moon dust is sharp-edged and sticks strongly.

80270.q: How long does light take to travel from the Moon to the Earth?
80270.e: Light is very fast. It takes only about 1.3 seconds to get from the Moon to us.
80270.m: Moonlight reaches us in just over a second.

80271.q: What is the faint glow of the dark part next to a thin crescent moon called?
80271.e: The Earth reflects sunlight back to the Moon. This light makes the dark part of the Moon a little bright.
80271.m: Earthshine is sunlight that the Earth reflects back to the Moon.

a: Yes, it even makes you hot
80272.e: Moonlight is much weaker than sunlight. You cannot feel its warmth on your skin.
80272.m: Moonlight is too weak to warm us.

80273.q: At which phase of the Moon is the night brightest?
80273.e: At full moon, the Moon reflects the most sunlight to the Earth. Outside you can even see shadows then.
80273.m: Nights are brightest at full moon.

80274.q: What do colours look like in bright moonlight?
a: Much more colourful than in the day
Exactly the same as in the day
80274.e: When there is little light, our eyes mainly use cells that cannot tell colours apart. That is why many things look grey in moonlight.
80274.m: In moonlight we hardly see colours.

80275.q: What is a rainbow called that appears at night in moonlight?
80275.e: When the bright Moon shines on raindrops, a faint rainbow can appear. It usually looks almost white.
80275.m: The Moon can make a rainbow too.

80276.q: How bright is the surface of the Moon really?
a: Rather dark, similar to old tarmac
80276.e: The Moon reflects only about an eighth of the sunlight. It only looks bright because the night sky around it is so dark.
80276.m: The surface of the Moon is actually quite dark.

80277.q: What is the bright glow called that sometimes lies close around the Moon when thin clouds pass in front of it?
80277.e: A lunar corona appears when moonlight shines through tiny water droplets in thin clouds. It lies close around the Moon.
80277.m: A lunar corona appears in thin clouds in front of the Moon.

80278.q: What is it called when the sea water goes back from the coast?
80278.e: At low tide the water level of the sea drops. The beach then becomes wider.
80278.m: At low tide the sea goes out.

80279.q: What is it called when the sea water rises at the coast?
80279.e: At high tide the water level rises. The sea comes closer to the coast.
80279.m: At high tide the water rises.

80280.q: Why is walking on the mudflats without a guide dangerous?
a: The tide can come back quickly
80280.e: The water returns at high tide and quickly fills the channels. Anyone who does not know the way can be cut off by the water.
80280.m: Only go onto the mudflats with a guide.

80281.q: Can you notice tides in Swiss lakes?
a: No, the lakes are too small
Yes, but only at full moon
80281.e: Tides are only clear in very large bodies of water such as the oceans. In our lakes the difference is tiny.
80281.m: You cannot notice tides in Swiss lakes.

80282.q: When is the difference between low and high tide especially large?
a: At full moon and new moon
80282.e: At full moon and new moon, the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a line. Then the Sun and the Moon pull on the water together.
80282.m: At full and new moon the tide rises especially high.

80283.q: Which animal lives in the mudflats and leaves little piles of sand?
80283.e: The lugworm lives in a tube in the sand. It passes out the sand it eats as little coiled piles.
80283.m: The coils of sand on the mudflats come from the lugworm.

80284.q: Roughly how long is it from one high tide to the next?
80284.e: There are about 12 hours and 25 minutes between two high tides. That is why there are usually two high tides a day.
80284.m: High tide comes about every twelve hours.

80285.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module?
80285.e: The module was called “Eagle”. The first people landed on the Moon in it in 1969.
80285.m: The first lunar module was called Eagle.

80286.q: How many astronauts flew down to the Moon in the lunar module each time?
80286.e: Two astronauts climbed into the module and landed. A colleague stayed in the spacecraft in orbit around the Moon.
80286.m: Two astronauts always landed in the lunar module.

80287.q: How many landing legs did the lunar module have?
80287.e: The module stood on four legs with round plates as feet. That way it did not sink into the Moon dust.
80287.m: The lunar module stood on four legs.

80288.q: Which part of the lunar module stayed behind on the Moon?
80288.e: The lower part with the legs served as a launch pad for the return. Only the upper part with the astronauts flew back up.
80288.m: The lower part of the lunar module stayed on the Moon.

80289.q: Could the lunar module land on the Earth?
a: No, it was built only for space
80289.e: The module was built very lightly and had no heat shield. The astronauts returned to Earth in a different capsule.
80289.m: The lunar module never flew back to Earth.

80290.q: What does the plaque on the leg of the Apollo 11 module on the Moon say?
a: We came in peace for all mankind
Have a good trip to Mars
80290.e: The plaque says “We came in peace for all mankind”. It is fixed to the lower part of the module, which stayed on the Moon.
80290.m: The Apollo 11 plaque speaks of peace for all people.

80291.q: On which mission did the lunar module serve as a lifeboat?
80291.e: On Apollo 13 an oxygen tank exploded on the way. The three astronauts survived in the lunar module and returned safely to Earth.
80291.m: On Apollo 13 the lunar module saved the astronauts.

80292.q: How many lunar modules landed on the Moon with people?
80292.e: From 1969 to 1972, six Apollo modules landed on the Moon. With two astronauts each, that made twelve people.
80292.m: Six Apollo modules landed on the Moon.

80293.q: Did the lunar module have seats for the astronauts?
80293.e: To save weight, there were no seats. The astronauts stood and were held in place with straps.
80293.m: In the lunar module the astronauts flew standing up.

80294.q: What did the Apollo 11 astronauts leave on the Moon that scientists still use today?
80294.e: From Earth, scientists send laser beams to this mirror. From the time it takes the light to come back, they work out the distance to the Moon.
80294.m: A mirror on the Moon is used to measure the distance to the Earth.

80295.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in the spacecraft in orbit around the Moon?
80295.e: Michael Collins flew around the Moon alone while his two colleagues landed. He never set foot on the Moon.
80295.m: Michael Collins waited in the spacecraft orbiting the Moon.

80296.q: Roughly how long were Armstrong and Aldrin out walking on the Moon?
a: About two and a half hours
80296.e: The trip on the surface of the Moon lasted about 2 hours and 31 minutes. Then the two climbed back into the lunar module.
80296.m: The first moonwalk lasted about two and a half hours.

80297.q: What did the Apollo 11 astronauts set up on the Moon?
80297.e: Armstrong and Aldrin put the flag of the United States into the Moon's ground. They also set up measuring instruments.
80297.m: There is a flag of the USA on the Moon.

80298.q: Roughly how long did the whole Apollo 11 journey take?
80298.e: Apollo 11 took off on 16 July and landed back on Earth on 24 July. That is about 8 days.
80298.m: The Apollo 11 trip to the Moon took about eight days.

80299.q: How many astronauts flew to the Moon on Apollo 11?
80299.e: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins flew to the Moon on Apollo 11 in 1969. Two of them landed on the Moon.
80299.m: Three astronauts flew to the Moon on Apollo 11.

80300.q: How does the famous sentence go on: “That's one small step for man, ...”?
80300.e: Neil Armstrong said this sentence when he became the first person to step onto the Moon.
80300.m: The first step on the Moon was a giant leap for mankind.

80301.q: How many people watched the Moon landing live on television?
80301.e: The pictures from the Moon were shown on television all over the world. It is estimated that around 600 million people watched.
80301.m: Hundreds of millions of people watched the Moon landing.

80302.q: What is the Lunar Roving Vehicle often called for short?
80302.e: The Lunar Roving Vehicle was a small vehicle for the Moon. It is often called the moon buggy.
80302.m: The Lunar Roving Vehicle is also called the moon buggy.

80303.q: How many wheels did the moon buggy of the Apollo missions have?
80303.e: The moon buggy ran on four wheels. Each wheel had its own small electric motor.
80303.m: The moon buggy had four wheels.

80304.q: What did the moon buggy run on?
80304.e: On the Moon there is no air to burn petrol. That is why the moon buggy had batteries and electric motors.
80304.m: The moon buggy ran on battery power.

80305.q: What did the astronauts need the moon buggy for?
80305.e: On foot, the astronauts could not get far on the Moon. With the moon buggy they could visit places further away and collect stones.
80305.m: With the moon buggy the astronauts could get around further.

80306.q: What were the wheels of the moon buggy made of?
80306.e: Air-filled tyres would have caused problems in space. So the wheels were made of a net of fine steel wire.
80306.m: The wheels of the moon buggy were made of wire mesh.

80307.q: How many moon buggies are still on the Moon today?
80307.e: Apollo 15, 16 and 17 left their moon buggies behind on the Moon. They are still there.
80307.m: Three moon buggies are still on the Moon.

80308.q: How many astronauts could fit in the moon buggy?
80308.e: The moon buggy had two seats side by side. The two astronauts drove it to places further away.
80308.m: Two astronauts sat in the moon buggy.

80309.q: Roughly what was the top speed of the moon buggy?
80309.e: The moon buggy was about as fast as a leisurely bike ride. Apollo 17 set the record at around 18 km/h.
80309.m: The moon buggy was about as fast as a bike.

a: A place where water comes out of the ground
A lake high up in the mountains
A place where a river ends
80310.e: At a spring, water comes out of the ground or out of a rock into the daylight. A stream often starts there.
80310.m: At a spring, water comes out of the earth.

80311.q: Why is spring water often cool even in summer?
a: It comes from the cool ground
It flows over blocks of ice
It falls from the sky at night
80311.e: Deep in the ground it stays about equally cool all year. That is why spring water is pleasantly fresh even on hot days.
80311.m: Spring water comes up cool from deep down.

80312.q: What is a spring called that warm water comes out of?
80312.e: The water of a thermal spring is heated deep inside the Earth. In Switzerland there are such springs in Baden or Leukerbad, for example.
80312.m: Warm water bubbles out of a thermal spring.

80313.q: What is a hot spring called that shoots water high into the air again and again?
80313.e: In a geyser, water underground gets so hot that it shoots upwards with steam. There are famous geysers in Iceland.
80313.m: A geyser shoots hot water into the air.

80314.q: Where does the water of the Rhône come from right at the start?
80314.e: The Rhône begins with meltwater from the Rhône Glacier in the canton of Valais.
80314.m: The Rhône begins at the Rhône Glacier in Valais.

80315.q: What is spring water with lots of dissolved minerals called that you can buy in bottles?
80315.e: On its way through the rock, water picks up minerals. Spring water like this is bottled and sold as mineral water.
80315.m: Mineral water comes from a spring.

80316.q: Can a spring dry up in summer?
a: Yes, if it does not rain for a long time
80316.e: A spring is fed by rain and snow that soak into the ground. If there is no rain for a long time, it can give less water or dry up completely.
80316.m: Without rain a spring can dry up.

80317.q: Where is the source of a river?
80317.e: A river begins at its source and then flows downhill. At the end it flows into another river, a lake or the sea.
80317.m: A river begins at its source.

a: A small body of flowing water
80318.e: A stream is smaller and narrower than a river. Its water keeps on flowing.
80318.m: A stream is a small body of flowing water.

80319.q: What forms when lots of streams flow together?
80319.e: Streams join together and get bigger and bigger. This is how a river forms.
80319.m: Lots of streams make a river.

80320.q: Which fish likes living in cool, clean streams?
80320.e: The brown trout needs cool water with lots of oxygen. It lives in many Swiss streams. Carp and catfish prefer warm, calm water.
80320.m: The trout likes cool, clean water.

80321.q: Which little creature under the stones in a stream shows that the water is clean?
80321.e: Freshwater shrimps need clean water with lots of oxygen. If you find lots of them, the stream is healthy.
80321.m: Lots of freshwater shrimps show the water is clean.

80322.q: Which bird dives in streams for small creatures?
80322.e: The dipper is a small songbird. It dives and even walks underwater along the bed of the stream.
80322.m: The dipper dives in streams for food.

80323.q: Which way does a stream flow?
80323.e: Because of gravity, water always flows downwards. That is why a stream flows downhill.

80324.q: Why does a mountain stream often flow very fast?
80324.e: The steeper the ground, the faster the water flows. In the mountains it is often very steep.
80324.m: The steeper the slope, the faster the stream.

80325.q: Which plant with yellow flowers likes to grow on wet stream banks in spring?
80325.e: The marsh marigold loves wet ground by streams and ditches. In spring its yellow flowers shine.
80325.m: The marsh marigold flowers yellow on stream banks.

80326.q: What does a beaver build in a stream?
80326.e: The beaver blocks the stream with branches and mud. This makes a pond where it can build its lodge safely.

a: Water that plunges over a rock step
Water that comes out of the ground
80327.e: In a waterfall, a stream or river flows over a steep step and falls down.
80327.m: A waterfall plunges down over a rock step.

80328.q: What can you often see in the fine spray of a waterfall when the sun is shining?
80328.e: The sun shines into the many tiny drops of water. These split the light into its colours.
80328.m: A rainbow often appears in the spray of a waterfall.

80329.q: What are the famous waterfalls between Canada and the USA called?
80329.e: Niagara Falls lie on the border between Canada and the USA. Millions of people visit them every year.
80329.m: Niagara Falls lie between Canada and the USA.

80330.q: What is the highest waterfall in the world called?
80330.e: Angel Falls is in Venezuela in South America. Its water falls almost 1000 metres.
80330.m: The highest waterfall in the world is Angel Falls.

80331.q: Which Swiss waterfalls plunge down inside a mountain?
80331.e: The Trümmelbach Falls thunder through a gorge inside the mountain near Lauterbrunnen. A lift takes visitors inside.
80331.m: The Trümmelbach Falls roar inside a mountain.

80332.q: What can the power of falling water be used for?
80332.e: Falling water drives turbines that make electricity. In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower.

80333.q: What is it called when people climb up frozen waterfalls in winter?
80333.e: In ice climbing, you climb up frozen waterfalls with ice axes and crampons. You only do this with training and safety ropes.
80333.m: You can go ice climbing on frozen waterfalls.

80334.q: Which village is the Staubbach Falls near?
80334.e: The Staubbach Falls plunge over a cliff into the valley right by the village of Lauterbrunnen.
80334.m: The Staubbach Falls are at Lauterbrunnen.

80335.q: Which canton are the Staubbach Falls in?
80335.e: The Staubbach Falls are in the Bernese Oberland, which is in the canton of Bern.
80335.m: The Staubbach Falls are in the canton of Bern.

80336.q: Roughly how high are the Staubbach Falls?
80336.e: The water of the Staubbach falls about 297 metres. It is one of the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.
80336.m: The Staubbach Falls are almost 300 metres high.

80337.q: Why are the Staubbach Falls called that? (“Staub” means dust in German.)
a: The water breaks up into fine droplets
They bring lots of dust into the valley
80337.e: On its long way down, the wind scatters the water in all directions. It then looks like fine dust.
80337.m: At the Staubbach Falls, the water turns into spray like dust.

80338.q: Which famous poet wrote a poem at the Staubbach Falls in 1779?
80338.e: Goethe visited the Staubbach Falls on a journey through Switzerland. There he wrote the poem “Song of the Spirits over the Waters”.
80338.m: Goethe wrote a poem at the Staubbach Falls.

80339.q: How can you get close to the Staubbach Falls in summer?
a: Through a gallery in the rock
By a lift in a tower
80339.e: In summer a path leads to a rock gallery at the Staubbach Falls. At other times the path is closed because of falling ice and rocks.
80339.m: In summer a path leads up to the Staubbach Falls.

80340.q: How does the water fall at the Staubbach Falls?
80340.e: The water plunges almost freely from the edge of the cliff. On the way down it turns into fine spray.
80340.m: The Staubbach falls freely over a cliff.

80341.q: When does the Staubbach carry the most water?
a: In early summer when the snow melts
80341.e: When the snow in the mountains melts in early summer, especially large amounts of water flow into the streams. In winter much of it is frozen.
80341.m: When the snow melts, mountain streams carry lots of water.

80342.q: Where does most of the drinking water in Switzerland come from?
80342.e: About 80 per cent of Swiss drinking water comes from groundwater and springs. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
80342.m: Most of Switzerland's drinking water comes from groundwater.

80343.q: What is used today to bring groundwater up from deep down?
80343.e: Pumps suck the groundwater up through pipes. Then it flows into the water mains.

80344.q: Why is groundwater often very clean?
80344.e: On its way through soil, sand and gravel, lots of bits of dirt get caught. The ground works like a filter.

a: Poison or too much fertiliser in the soil
80345.e: Whatever soaks into the ground can reach the groundwater. That is why you must never pour poison or oil onto the ground.
80345.m: Poison in the soil can pollute groundwater.

80346.q: How did people long ago get water up from a deep well?
a: With a bucket on a rope
80346.e: A well like this reaches down to the groundwater. People lowered a bucket on a rope and pulled it back up full of water.
80346.m: People used to get well water up with a bucket.

80347.q: Where in the ground is groundwater usually found?
a: In gaps between gravel and sand
In big caves full of air
80347.e: Groundwater fills the tiny spaces between small stones, gravel and sand. There is usually no open underground lake.
80347.m: Groundwater is in the gaps between gravel and sand.

a: Yes, as fast as a river
80348.e: Groundwater moves slowly through the ground, often only a few metres a day. It flows towards rivers or lakes.

80349.q: What happens to groundwater if it does not rain for a very long time?
a: It gets as warm as a bath
80349.e: Without rain, no new water comes in. The water table then slowly drops.
80349.m: In a drought, the groundwater sinks.

a: When the ground is completely dry
80350.e: Rainwater flows into small dips in the ground. If it cannot soak away quickly, a puddle is left.
80350.m: Puddles collect in dips after rain.

80351.q: Why do puddles on tarmac stay for a long time?
a: Tarmac does not let water through
80351.e: Tarmac is sealed, so the water cannot soak into the ground. It stays there until it evaporates or drains away.
80351.m: Tarmac does not let rainwater through.

80352.q: Where does a puddle go on a sunny day?
a: A bird drinks it all up
80352.e: The warmth of the sun makes the water evaporate. It becomes invisible water vapour in the air.

80353.q: What shimmers in a puddle when a little oil is floating on it?
80353.e: A very thin layer of oil on the water makes the light shimmer in bright colours.
80353.m: Oil on a puddle shimmers in many colours.

80354.q: What happens to a puddle on a frosty night?
80354.e: Below 0 degrees, water turns into ice. In the morning the puddle is then often covered with a layer of ice.
80354.m: Puddles freeze when there is frost.

80355.q: Which birds collect wet mud from puddles to build their nests?
80355.e: Swallows make little balls out of damp mud. They use them to stick their nests under a roof, for example.
80355.m: Swallows build their nests from mud.

80356.q: What do you see when you look into a still puddle?
80356.e: The smooth surface of the water reflects the light like a mirror. That is why you see yourself and the sky.
80356.m: A still puddle reflects like a mirror.

80357.q: Which insects like to lay their eggs in puddles and water butts?
80357.e: Mosquitoes need still water for their larvae. Even a small puddle can be enough.
80357.m: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water.

80358.q: Which animals sometimes lay their eggs in puddles in wheel ruts?
80358.e: Some toads, such as the yellow-bellied toad, like small, warm puddles, for example in wheel ruts. They lay their spawn there.
80358.m: Toads also lay their eggs in puddles.

80359.q: On which nights does a lot of dew form?
80359.e: Without clouds, the ground cools down a lot at night. Without wind, the water from the air can then settle easily on the grass.
80359.m: Clear, calm nights bring lots of dew.

80360.q: Where does the water in dewdrops come from?
a: From water vapour in the air
80360.e: There is invisible water vapour in the air. When the air cools down, it turns back into liquid water in small drops.
80360.m: Dew forms from water vapour in the air.

80361.q: What happens to dew when the sun shines in the morning?
a: It turns into fog in the ground
80361.e: The sun warms the grass and the air. The drops then turn back into water vapour.

80362.q: Where do dewdrops glitter especially beautifully in the morning?
80362.e: Lots of little drops hang on the fine threads of a spider's web. In the morning light they glitter like pearls.
80362.m: Dewdrops glitter like pearls on spiders' webs.

80363.q: What happens to cold glasses when you come into a warm room?
a: They steam up with tiny droplets
80363.e: The warm air in the room contains water vapour. On the cold glasses it turns into tiny drops, just like dew.
80363.m: Water droplets form on cold surfaces.

80364.q: On a clear night, when is it usually coolest?
80364.e: The ground cools down all night long. That is why it is usually coldest at sunrise, and there is lots of dew.
80364.m: It is often coolest at sunrise.

80365.q: Why is there often less dew under a tree in the morning?
a: The ground there cools down less
The sun shines there at night
80365.e: The treetop works like a blanket and holds back some warmth. The ground underneath gets less cold, so less dew forms.
80365.m: Under trees it cools down less and there is less dew.

a: Fine ice crystals on branches and grass
80366.e: Hoar frost is made of lots of tiny ice crystals. They grow on trees, fences and grass.
80366.m: Hoar frost is made of fine ice crystals.

80367.q: In what weather does hoar frost form?
a: When it is frosty and the air is damp
When it is hot and sunny
80367.e: Hoar frost forms when it is colder than 0 degrees and the air is damp, for example in fog. The tiny droplets freeze onto everything they touch.
80367.m: Hoar frost needs frost and damp air.

80368.e: The many fine ice crystals scatter the light. That is why hoar frost looks white.

80369.q: In which season do we see hoar frost in Switzerland?
80369.e: Hoar frost needs temperatures below 0 degrees. In Switzerland that happens mainly in winter and on cold autumn nights.
80369.m: You see hoar frost mainly in winter.

80370.q: On which side of the twigs does hoar frost grow most?
a: On the side the wind comes from
On the side facing the ground
80370.e: The wind carries the damp, cold air against the twigs. Where it hits them, the ice crystals grow the most.
80370.m: Hoar frost grows towards the wind.

80371.q: What are the patterns of ice called that grow on cold window panes?
80371.e: On cold panes the moisture freezes into branching patterns. They look like flowers made of ice.
80371.m: Frost flowers are ice patterns on windows.

80372.q: What can happen when a lot of hoar frost hangs on trees?
80372.e: Thick hoar frost can get very heavy. Then the branches bend and some break off.
80372.m: Heavy hoar frost can break branches.

80373.q: What happens to hoar frost when it gets warmer?
80373.e: When the temperature rises above 0 degrees, the ice crystals melt. They often fall off the branches like fine snow, too.
80373.m: Hoar frost melts when it gets warmer.

a: Dripping water freezes bit by bit
80374.e: Water runs down an edge and freezes drop by drop. This makes the icicle longer and longer.

80375.q: Why is it dangerous to walk under big icicles?
80375.e: Big icicles are heavy and pointed. If they come loose, they can hurt people.
80375.m: It is better not to walk under big icicles.

80376.q: In what weather do icicles grow especially well?
a: The sun melts snow, but the air is cold
80376.e: The sun melts some snow on the roof. The water drips down and freezes into ice in the cold air.
80376.m: Icicles grow when melting snow freezes in cold air.

80377.q: Which way do icicles grow on a roof?
80377.e: Because of gravity, the water drips downwards. That is why icicles grow from the top down.

80378.q: What happens to icicles when it thaws?
a: They get as hard as stone
80378.e: When it gets warmer than 0 degrees, the ice melts. The icicles drip and get smaller until they fall off.

80379.q: Why are icicles pointed at the bottom?
a: The least water reaches the bottom
Birds peck them into a point
80379.e: Most of the water freezes further up the icicle. Only a little reaches the tip, so it stays thin.
80379.m: Icicles are thick at the top and pointed at the bottom.

80380.q: Where in nature can very long icicles hang in winter?
80380.e: In winter, water seeps out of cracks in the rocks. It freezes and sometimes forms icicles several metres long.
80380.m: Huge icicles grow on rock faces in winter.

a: A very wet area with soft ground
80381.e: In a bog the ground is full of water and very soft. You can sink into it.
80381.m: A bog is a wet area with soft ground.

80382.q: Which animals like living in a wet bog?
80382.e: In a bog there is lots of water and lots of insects. That is why frogs feel at home there.

80383.q: Why are many bogs in Switzerland protected?
a: Rare plants and animals live there
Lots of vegetables are grown there
The best ski slopes are there
Most of the timber grows there
80383.e: In bogs there are plants and animals that are hardly found anywhere else. That is why many bogs are protected.
80383.m: Bogs are home to rare plants and animals.

80384.q: Which small meat-eating plant grows in Swiss bogs?
80384.e: The sundew has sticky drops on its leaves. Small insects get stuck to them and are digested.
80384.m: The sundew catches insects with sticky drops.

80385.q: Who decided in 1987 that bogs in Switzerland should be specially protected?
80385.e: In the vote on the Rothenthurm initiative, the people said yes to protecting bogs. Since then this has been in the Federal Constitution.
80385.m: The Swiss people decided to protect bogs in 1987.

80386.q: Why can a bog store so much water?
a: The moss soaks up water like a sponge
The ground is made of hard rock
Lots of big trees grow there
80386.e: Peat moss can hold many times its own weight in water. This is how the bog holds on to lots of water.
80386.m: A bog stores water like a sponge.

80387.q: Why should you stay on the paths in a bog?
a: You can sink in and trample plants
It is warmer on the paths
It is too dark beside the paths
80387.e: The soft ground of the bog cannot hold you everywhere. Also, rare plants grow there that are easily damaged.
80387.m: In a bog, you stay on the paths.

80388.q: What colour is the water in a raised bog often?
80388.e: Substances from dead plants dissolve in the water. They turn it brown like tea.
80388.m: Bog water is often brown like tea.

a: A small, shallow body of still water
80389.e: A pond is small and so shallow that plants often grow right down to the bottom. The water hardly flows.
80389.m: A pond is a small, shallow body of water.

80390.q: Which animals lay their spawn in the pond in spring?
80390.e: Frogs lay their eggs in the water as spawn. The clumps of eggs float in the pond.
80390.m: Frogs lay spawn in the pond in spring.

80391.q: What are young frogs called that still live in the water?
80391.e: Tadpoles hatch from frogspawn. They have a tail and breathe with gills until they become frogs.

80392.q: Which insect with shimmering wings hunts mosquitoes over ponds?
80392.e: Dragonflies are fast fliers and catch other insects in the air. Their larvae live in the water.
80392.m: Dragonflies hunt mosquitoes over the water.

80393.q: Which insect can walk on the surface of the water?
80393.e: The pond skater is very light and has long legs with fine hairs. That is why it does not sink.
80393.m: The pond skater walks on water.

80394.q: Which plant with big round leaves floats on ponds?
80394.e: The water lily has its roots in the mud at the bottom. Its leaves and flowers float on the water.
80394.m: The water lily floats on the pond.

80395.q: Which plant on the edge of a pond has brown heads that look like sausages?
80395.e: The bulrush grows in shallow water at the edge. Its brown heads are full of seeds.
80395.m: The bulrush has brown heads at the water's edge.

80396.q: Why does a pond freeze over faster in winter than a big lake?
a: It is always in a forest
80396.e: A small, shallow pond holds little water. It cools down quickly and therefore freezes over sooner than a big, deep lake.
80396.m: Small, shallow ponds freeze over quickly.

80397.q: Which bird often swims on ponds, with the male having a shiny green head?
80397.e: The mallard is the most common duck in Switzerland. You can recognise the male by its shimmering green head.
80397.m: The male mallard has a green head.

80398.q: Why can you not drink seawater?
80398.e: Seawater contains a lot of salt. If you drink it, you get even thirstier, because your body has to get rid of the salt.
80398.m: Seawater is too salty to drink.

80399.q: Is there more sea or more land on Earth?
80399.e: Most of the Earth is covered by sea. That is why the Earth is also called the blue planet.
80399.m: Most of the Earth is covered by sea.

80400.q: Which sea does the Rhine flow into in the end?
80400.e: The Rhine flows from Switzerland through Germany and the Netherlands. There it flows into the North Sea.
80400.m: The Rhine flows into the North Sea.

80401.q: Which sea does the Rhône flow into in the end?
80401.e: The Rhône flows through Lake Geneva and then through France. It flows into the Mediterranean in southern France.
80401.m: The Rhône flows into the Mediterranean.

80402.q: Which sea does the water of the Inn from the Engadine reach?
80402.e: The Inn flows into the Danube. The Danube finally flows into the Black Sea.
80402.m: The water of the Inn reaches the Black Sea.

80403.q: What is the largest animal in the sea?
80403.e: The blue whale can grow over 30 metres long. It is even the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth.
80403.m: The blue whale is the largest animal in the world.

80405.q: What do you do with finely chopped red cabbage to get red cabbage juice?
80405.e: The hot water draws the colour out of the leaves. After cooling, you pour the coloured juice through a sieve.
80405.m: Hot water draws the colour out of red cabbage.

80406.q: What colour is red cabbage juice in pure water?
80406.e: In water that is neither acidic nor basic, red cabbage juice is purple. Only when you add something does the colour change.
80406.m: In pure water, red cabbage juice is purple.

80407.q: What colour does red cabbage juice turn when you stir in bicarbonate of soda?
80407.e: Bicarbonate of soda is not acidic but basic. That is why the purple red cabbage juice turns blue to blue-green.
80407.m: Bicarbonate of soda turns red cabbage juice blue.

80408.q: What does red cabbage juice show with its colour?
80408.e: The dye in red cabbage changes colour depending on whether a substance is acidic or basic. This lets you test things from the kitchen.
80408.m: Red cabbage juice shows by its colour whether something is acidic.

80409.q: What do you call a substance that shows by its colour whether something is acidic?
80409.e: An indicator is something that shows. Red cabbage juice is an indicator you can make yourself.
80409.m: An indicator shows by its colour whether something is acidic.

80410.q: What does a splash of vinegar do to the colour when cooking red cabbage?
80410.e: Acid from vinegar or sour apples keeps red cabbage red. Without acid it tends to turn bluish when cooked.
80410.m: With a little acid, cooked red cabbage stays red.

80411.q: What property does lemon juice have if it turns red cabbage juice red?
80411.e: Lemon juice contains acid. Acidic substances turn red cabbage juice red.
80411.m: Acidic substances turn red cabbage juice red.

80412.q: Which juice, like red cabbage juice, changes colour with acid?
80412.e: Blueberries contain a blue dye similar to red cabbage. That is why their juice also changes colour with acid.
80412.m: Blueberry juice also changes colour with acid.

80413.q: What is food colouring used for?
80413.e: Food colouring is safe to eat. It is used, for example, to colour cakes, icing or Easter eggs.

80414.q: Which colour do you get when you mix red and yellow food colouring?
80414.e: Red and yellow together make orange. This way you can mix many new colours from just a few.
80414.m: Red and yellow together make orange.

80415.q: Which vegetable colours food bright red?
80415.e: Beetroot contains a strong red dye. Hands and clothes quickly turn red from it too.

80416.e: Turmeric is a yellow powder made from a root. It colours curries yellow, for example.

80417.q: In which water does a drop of food colouring spread faster?
80417.e: In warm water the tiniest particles move faster. That is why the colour spreads more quickly there.
80417.m: Colour spreads faster in warm water than in cold.

80418.q: What happens to a white flower that stands in water with food colouring for a few days?
a: The flower loses all its leaves
The flower grows twice as big
80418.e: The flower sucks the coloured water up through its stem. This way the colour reaches the flower head.
80418.m: A flower sucks water up through its stem to the flower head.

80419.q: Which vegetable provides a green colouring for food?
80419.e: Spinach contains a lot of green leaf pigment. You can use spinach to colour pasta green, for example.

80420.q: Which letter do the numbers of colourings on packaging start with?
80420.e: Additives such as colourings have an E number on packaging. Colourings have the numbers E 100 to E 199.
80420.m: Colourings are listed on packaging with an E number.

80421.q: You want to separate the colours of a felt-tip pen with water. Which paper do you put the dot of colour on?
80421.e: Coffee filter paper soaks up water well. The water can travel upwards in it and carry the colours with it.
80421.m: To separate colours, you need paper that soaks up water well.

80422.q: A coffee filter with a felt-tip dot stands in water. What travels up the paper and takes the colour with it?
80422.e: The paper soaks water up from the glass. The water dissolves the colour and carries it along.
80422.m: The water carries the colours up the paper.

80423.q: You draw a dot with a black felt-tip pen on a coffee filter and stand it in water. What do you soon see?
a: No colour at all any more
80423.e: Black felt-tip ink is often mixed from several colours. On the paper they separate, for example into blue, yellow and red.
80423.m: Black ink is often mixed from several colours.

80424.q: Where must the dot of colour be on the paper strip when it goes into the water?
80424.e: If the dot is in the water, the colour simply dissolves in the glass. If it is just above, the water rises up to it.
80424.m: The dot of colour must be just above the water.

80425.q: Which pens can you use to separate colours in paper with water?
80425.e: The colour must dissolve in water, otherwise it just stays put. That is why washable felt-tip pens work best.
80425.m: To separate colours with water, you need washable felt-tip pens.

80426.q: What does the Greek word ‘chroma’ in chromatography mean?
80426.e: ‘Chroma’ is the Greek word for colour. So chromatography means roughly ‘colour writing’.

80427.q: A coffee filter with a felt-tip dot stands in water. Why do different stripes of colour appear?
80427.e: Some colours are easily carried along by the water, others tend to stay behind. So they get different distances and separate.
80427.m: Each colour travels a different distance in the paper.

80428.q: Which pigments can you separate from green leaves with chromatography?
80428.e: Green leaves contain not only green but also yellow pigment. With methylated spirits instead of water, and with the help of an adult, you can separate them.
80428.m: Green leaves also contain yellow pigment.

80429.q: What can you use to make a simple invisible ink?
80429.e: Lemon juice is almost colourless and hard to see once dry. That is why it works well as invisible ink.
80429.m: Lemon juice is a simple invisible ink.

80430.q: How do you make writing in lemon juice visible again?
80430.e: When the paper is carefully warmed, for example with an iron, the dried juice changes colour. Only do this with an adult.
80430.m: Heat makes secret writing in lemon juice visible.

80431.q: What colour does lemon juice writing turn when heated?
80431.e: The juice contains sugar and other substances. When heated they turn brown, a bit like toast.

80432.q: Which drink from the fridge can also be an invisible ink?
80432.e: Dried milk is hard to see on white paper. When carefully warmed it turns brown and the writing appears.
80432.m: Milk can also be used as invisible ink.

80433.q: You write with a white candle on white paper. How do you make the writing visible?
80433.e: Wax repels water. The watercolour stays on the paper but not on the wax letters, so they show up light.
80433.m: Wax repels watercolour, so candle writing appears.

80434.q: What is the best thing to write on paper with lemon juice?
80434.e: You dip a cotton bud or a fine brush into the lemon juice and write with it. A pen would leave visible lines.
80434.m: Secret writing in lemon juice is done with a cotton bud or brush.

80435.q: You write with bicarbonate of soda water and then brush red cabbage juice over it. What happens?
80435.e: The bicarbonate of soda changes the colour of the red cabbage juice. That is why the letters appear in a different colour from the rest of the paper.
80435.m: Red cabbage juice can make bicarbonate of soda writing visible.

80436.q: What did people use invisible ink for in the past?
80436.e: With invisible ink, messages could be hidden. Only those who knew how to make it visible could read them.
80436.m: Invisible ink hides messages from prying eyes.

80437.e: Soap is made by boiling fats or oils with an alkali. This boiling is called soap making.
80437.m: Soap is made from fat and alkali.

80438.q: Why do you wash your hands with soap instead of just water?
80438.e: Water alone is poor at rinsing away greasy dirt. Soap wraps up the grease so that the water can rinse it away.
80438.m: Soap helps water rinse away greasy dirt.

80439.q: You sprinkle pepper on water and dip in a finger covered in soap. What does the pepper do?
80439.e: The soap weakens the stretched skin on the surface of the water. The water pulls back towards the edge and takes the pepper with it.
80439.m: Soap weakens the skin on the water.

80440.q: What were the craftsmen who used to make soap called?
80440.e: Soap was boiled in large pots. That is why the craftsmen were called soap boilers.
80440.m: In the past, soap boilers boiled soap in large pots.

80441.q: What forms when you rub soap with a little water between your hands?
80441.e: Soap and water form lots of tiny bubbles when rubbed. You know this white lather from washing your hands.

80442.q: When should you wash your hands with soap especially well?
a: After the toilet and before eating
80442.e: After using the toilet and before eating, clean hands are especially important. That way fewer germs get into your mouth.
80442.m: Wash your hands with soap after the toilet and before eating.

80443.q: A little paper boat has a drop of soap at the back. What happens in the water?
80443.e: The soap weakens the skin on the water at the back. At the front the water pulls more strongly, so the boat moves forwards.
80443.m: A drop of soap can power a paper boat.

80444.q: What happens to a bar of soap that lies in a puddle of water for a long time?
80444.e: Water slowly dissolves the soap at its surface. That is why it is better to let soap dry after washing.
80444.m: Soap in water goes soft and slimy.

80445.q: What is a simple, unscented bar of soap that is also used to wash clothes called?
80445.e: Household soap is a simple, solid soap. It is used, for example, to wash stains out of clothes.
80445.m: Household soap is a simple solid soap.

80446.q: What shape is a soap bubble that floats freely through the air?
80446.e: The thin soap skin pulls itself together as small as possible. The shape with the smallest surface is the sphere.
80446.m: A freely floating soap bubble is perfectly round.

80447.q: What is inside a soap bubble?
80447.e: When you blow, you blow air into the soap skin. Only the thin skin is made of soapy water.
80447.m: A soap bubble is full of air.

80448.q: Why does a soap bubble shimmer in many colours?
a: Light is reflected in the thin skin
80448.e: Light is reflected from the front and back of the thin soap skin. This creates shimmering rainbow colours.
80448.m: The thin skin of a soap bubble makes rainbow colours.

80449.q: What do you add to soapy water so that soap bubbles last longer?
80449.e: Glycerine is a thick, clear liquid. It stops the soap skin from drying out so quickly.
80449.m: Glycerine makes soap bubbles last longer.

80450.q: Why does a soap bubble burst after a while?
80450.e: The water in the soap skin evaporates and flows downwards. When the skin gets too thin, the bubble bursts.
80450.m: A soap bubble bursts when its skin gets too thin.

80451.q: What often happens if you carefully poke a soap bubble with a wet, soapy finger?
80451.e: A dry finger makes the bubble burst. But a finger with soapy water joins up with the soap skin.
80451.m: You can touch a soap bubble with a wet, soapy finger.

80452.q: What can happen to a soap bubble in very cold weather?
80452.e: In hard frost, the water in the soap skin freezes. Then you can see delicate ice patterns on the bubble.
80452.m: In hard frost, soap bubbles can freeze.

80453.q: About how thick is the skin of a soap bubble?
80453.e: The skin of a soap bubble is wafer-thin. It is much thinner than a human hair.
80453.m: The skin of a soap bubble is wafer-thin.

80454.q: What do you mix to make a simple bubble mixture?
80454.e: For soap bubbles you need water and something soapy such as washing-up liquid. Together they make a stretchy skin.
80454.m: Water and washing-up liquid make a bubble mixture.

80455.e: Foam is made of lots of bubbles full of air. Between the bubbles are thin walls of liquid.
80455.m: Foam is made of lots of little air bubbles.

80456.q: Which foam do you get when you beat egg white hard?
80456.e: When beating, air is stirred into the egg white. It turns white and stiff and is then called whisked egg white.
80456.m: Beaten egg white is called whisked egg white.

80457.q: What do you whip to make whipped cream?
80457.e: When whipping, air gets into the cream. The fat in the cream holds the bubbles in place.
80457.m: Whipping cream turns it into whipped cream.

80458.q: What do firefighters often use to put out burning petrol?
80458.e: The foam lies over the burning petrol like a blanket. Then no more air can reach the fire.

a: It contains a lot of flour
80459.e: Each bubble reflects a little light in all directions. Together the many bubbles look white, much like snow.
80459.m: Lots of little bubbles make foam look white.

80460.q: Where can you find solid foam?
80460.e: Foam rubber is solid foam with lots of air bubbles. That is why a mattress is soft and light.
80460.m: Foam rubber is solid foam full of air.

80461.q: Which drink often has a layer of milk froth on top?
80461.e: For a cappuccino, milk is frothed up with hot steam. The froth goes on top of the coffee.
80461.m: A cappuccino has milk froth on top.

80462.q: What happens to foam if you wait a long time?
80462.e: The thin walls of the bubbles get thinner over time and burst. That is why foam slowly sinks down.

80463.q: Why do you put washing-up liquid in the washing-up water?
a: It loosens the grease from the dishes
80463.e: Grease sticks to dishes and is hard to wash off with water alone. Washing-up liquid loosens the grease so the water can rinse it away.
80463.m: Washing-up liquid loosens grease from dishes.

80464.q: What happens if you add a little washing-up liquid to milk with drops of colour?
80464.e: The washing-up liquid changes the surface of the milk and loosens the milk fat. This sets the colours moving.
80464.m: Washing-up liquid sets drops of colour on milk moving.

80465.q: Why must ordinary washing-up liquid not go into the dishwasher?
a: It makes far too much foam
80465.e: Washing-up liquid foams a lot. In the machine the foam would pour out, so it needs its own product.
80465.m: Only dishwasher detergent goes into the dishwasher.

80466.q: You drip water onto a coin. What changes if there is washing-up liquid in the water?
a: Many more drops fit on it
80466.e: Pure water forms a high dome on the coin. Washing-up liquid weakens the skin of the water, so it overflows sooner.
80466.m: With washing-up liquid, water does not form such a high dome.

80467.q: What must you never do with washing-up liquid?
80467.e: Washing-up liquid is for cleaning, not for eating or drinking. Keep it where small children cannot reach it.

80468.q: How much washing-up liquid do you need for a bowl of washing-up water?
80468.e: Washing-up liquid works even in small amounts. Too much is unnecessary and pollutes the waste water.
80468.m: A few squirts of washing-up liquid are enough for the washing-up.

80469.q: Why should you put cream on your hands after a long time washing up?
a: Washing-up liquid dries out the skin
Washing-up liquid makes the skin hot
Washing-up liquid makes the skin thick
80469.e: Washing-up liquid removes not only grease from dishes but also the skin's natural oils. A cream gives the skin back its oils.
80469.m: Washing-up liquid can dry out the skin.

80471.q: What happens when you shake a bottle of oil and water hard?
80471.e: When shaken, the oil breaks up into lots of tiny droplets that float in the water. The liquid then looks cloudy.
80471.m: When shaken, oil in water breaks up into tiny droplets.

80472.q: What must you never use to put out burning oil in a pan?
80472.e: Water sinks under the hot oil, turns to steam at once and throws burning oil out. It is better to smother the fire with a lid.
80472.m: Never put out burning oil with water.

80473.q: Which sauce is made from oil and egg yolk that mix well?
80473.e: Egg yolk contains a substance that joins oil and water. That is why oil and egg yolk become a thick mayonnaise.
80473.m: Mayonnaise is a mixture of oil and egg yolk.

80474.q: In which drink are tiny droplets of fat spread through water?
80474.e: Milk is mostly water. Tiny droplets of fat float in it, which is why it is white and not see-through.
80474.m: Tiny droplets of fat float in milk.

80475.q: What do you call a mixture of tiny oil droplets in water?
80475.e: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix. One floats in tiny droplets in the other.
80475.m: A mixture of oil droplets in water is called an emulsion.

80476.q: What helps oil and water mix better?
80476.e: Washing-up liquid can cling to oil and to water at the same time. In this way it joins the two liquids.
80476.m: Washing-up liquid helps oil and water mix.

80477.q: Why can't you wash an oil stain out of a jumper with water alone?
a: Oil is too cold for it
80477.e: Water simply runs off the oil in beads. You need soap or detergent to loosen the oil.
80477.m: Wash oil stains with soap, not just with water.

80478.q: What do you do with a salad dressing of oil and vinegar just before serving?
80478.e: Oil and vinegar separate when the dressing stands. Shaking or stirring mixes them again.
80478.m: Shake a salad dressing well before serving.

80479.q: What makes the lumps of wax in a lava lamp rise?
80479.e: At the bottom of the lava lamp is a light bulb. It warms the wax, which expands, gets lighter and rises.
80479.m: In a lava lamp, heat makes the wax rise.

80480.q: What happens to the wax at the top of a lava lamp?
80480.e: It is cooler at the top than at the bottom. The wax cools, becomes heavier again and sinks back down.
80480.m: Cooled wax sinks down in a lava lamp.

80481.q: What do you see in a lava lamp?
a: Coloured blobs floating up and down
80481.e: In a lava lamp, soft, coloured blobs of wax float slowly upwards and back down again.
80481.m: In a lava lamp, blobs of wax float up and down.

80482.q: What makes the bubbles rise in a home-made lava lamp of water and oil?
80482.e: The effervescent tablet fizzes in the water and forms gas bubbles. These carry coloured drops of water upwards.
80482.m: An effervescent tablet makes a home-made lava lamp bubble.

80483.q: What does the food colouring colour in a home-made lava lamp of water and oil?
80483.e: Food colouring dissolves in water but not in oil. That is why the oil stays clear and only the water becomes coloured.
80483.m: Food colouring colours water but not oil.

80484.q: Why does it take a while for a real lava lamp to start bubbling after it is switched on?
a: The wax has to warm up first
The water has to freeze first
The lamp has to dry first
80484.e: At first the wax is solid and cold. Only when it is warm and soft do the blobs start to rise.
80484.m: A lava lamp needs time for the wax to warm up.

80485.q: Why should you not shake a warm lava lamp?
80485.e: When shaken, wax and liquid mix into tiny droplets. The lamp can then stay cloudy for a long time.
80485.m: Never shake a warm lava lamp.

80486.q: Where does the lava lamp get its name from?
a: It is filled with real lava
It was invented on a volcano
It gets as hot as lava
80486.e: The slowly flowing blobs of wax look like glowing lava from a volcano. That is why it is called a lava lamp.
80486.m: The wax blobs in a lava lamp look like lava.

80487.q: What can you easily use to grow crystals at home?
80487.e: You dissolve a lot of salt or sugar in water. As the water slowly evaporates, crystals grow from it.
80487.m: You can grow crystals from salt water or sugar water.

80488.q: Why do you dissolve the salt in warm water to grow crystals?
a: The salt turns colourful in it
The salt turns sweet in it
The salt goes hard in it
80488.e: Warm water can take up more salt than cold. The more salt is dissolved, the better the crystals grow.
80488.m: More salt dissolves in warm water.

80489.q: What do you hang in the salt solution so that crystals grow on it?
80489.e: You tie a piece of string to a pencil and lay the pencil across the glass. The crystals form on the string.
80489.m: Crystals grow on a string in the salt solution.

80490.q: How long does it take for nice crystals to grow?
80490.e: Crystals grow slowly while the water evaporates. So you need patience and should check every day.
80490.m: Growing crystals takes several days of patience.

80491.q: Where is the best place to put the glass with the crystal solution?
80491.e: Crystals grow best when the glass is not moved. Shaking disturbs their growth.
80491.m: Crystals grow best in a quiet place.

80492.q: What are the large sugar crystals you can put in tea called?
80492.e: Rock sugar forms when sugar slowly crystallises out of a solution. This produces large, clear crystals.
80492.m: Rock sugar is made of large sugar crystals.

80493.q: How many arms does a snow crystal have?
80493.e: Snow crystals are ice crystals. Because of the way ice is built, snowflakes have six arms or six points.
80493.m: A snow crystal has six arms.

80495.q: What is rock crystal made of?
80495.e: Rock crystal is clear, transparent quartz. Especially beautiful pieces are found in the Swiss Alps.
80495.m: Rock crystal is made of quartz.

80496.q: What colour is table salt in the tub?
80496.e: A single pure salt crystal is actually transparent. Lots of small grains together look white.

80497.q: Why did people in the past put meat and fish in salt?
80497.e: Salt draws water out of food. Without water, bacteria can hardly multiply, so salted food goes off less quickly.
80497.m: Salt makes meat and fish keep longer.

80498.q: Which animals like to lick a salt lick in the barn?
80498.e: Cows need salt, but they find too little of it in grass. That is why they get a salt lick in the barn or in the field.
80498.m: Cows like to lick a salt lick.

80499.q: Which bake is often sprinkled with coarse grains of salt?
80499.e: Pretzels are sprinkled with coarse salt before baking. The other bakes are usually sweet or have no salt crust.
80499.m: Pretzels are sprinkled with coarse salt.

80500.q: What is salt that is mined deep in the earth called?
80500.e: A very long time ago, seas dried up and left layers of salt behind. This salt in the ground is called rock salt.
80500.m: Salt from the earth is called rock salt.

80501.q: What do you use to sprinkle salt on your food at the table?
80501.e: A salt cellar has little holes at the top. That way only a little salt lands on the food.
80501.m: You season food at the table with a salt cellar.

80502.q: How much salt should you use with your food?
80502.e: The body needs some salt. But too much salt is unhealthy, so use it sparingly.

80504.q: Where does a tram get its electricity from?
a: From a wire above the street
80504.e: An overhead line hangs above the tram tracks. The tram gets the electricity for its motors from it.
80504.m: A tram gets its electricity from the wire above the street.

80505.q: Why can a tram not swerve around an obstacle?
80505.e: A tram is tied to its rails. That is why you must take special care on tram tracks.
80505.m: A tram cannot swerve because it runs on rails.

80506.q: How does a tram warn people in the street?
80506.e: Trams have a loud bell. When it rings, you should get off the tracks straight away.
80506.m: A tram warns with its bell.

80507.q: What colours are the trams in Zurich?
80507.e: Zurich’s trams are blue and white. These are also the colours of the city of Zurich.
80507.m: Zurich’s trams are blue and white.

80508.q: In which Swiss city do the green trams of the BVB run?
80508.e: The Basel transport company, BVB for short, has green trams. People in Basel affectionately call the tram “Drämmli”.

80509.q: What is the arm on the roof that collects electricity from the wire called?
80509.e: The pantograph presses against the overhead line from below. That way electricity flows into the tram.
80509.m: The pantograph collects electricity from the wire.

80510.q: Who has right of way when a tram crosses a zebra crossing?
80510.e: A tram has a long braking distance and cannot swerve. That is why in Switzerland pedestrians do not have right of way over a tram, even on a zebra crossing.
80510.m: Pedestrians do not have right of way over a tram.

80512.e: PostBuses in Switzerland are bright yellow. That is why you can spot them from far away.

80513.q: What is the PostBus horn with its three notes called?
80513.e: The horn plays three notes one after another. The tune comes from the overture to the opera “William Tell” by Gioachino Rossini.
80513.m: The PostBus has a three-tone horn.

80514.q: In which year did Switzerland’s first PostBus run?
80514.e: The first PostBus ran in 1906 between Bern and Detligen. Before that, coaches carried the post and the travellers.

80515.q: Who used to pull the mail coach before there were PostBuses?
80515.e: In the past, people and letters travelled in mail coaches. These were pulled by horses, even over the Alpine passes.
80515.m: Horses used to pull the mail coach.

80516.q: Who has right of way on a mountain postal road?
80516.e: On mountain roads with the sign “mountain postal road”, the PostBus has right of way. Other vehicles must make room for it.
80516.m: On a mountain postal road, the PostBus has right of way.

80517.q: Why does the PostBus sound its horn before tight bends on mountain roads?
80517.e: On tight bends you cannot see whether someone is coming the other way. The horn warns others that a big PostBus is coming.
80517.m: The PostBus sounds its horn on tight bends as a warning.

80518.q: Besides passengers, what did the PostBus use to bring?
80518.e: The PostBus belongs to Swiss Post. In the past, besides passengers, it also carried the post to the villages.
80518.m: The PostBus used to bring letters and parcels too.

80519.q: Where do PostBuses go especially often?
80519.e: PostBuses link many villages, valleys and passes where no train goes. That way you can get into the mountains even without a car.
80519.m: PostBuses go to many villages and mountain valleys.

80521.q: What is a lorry’s blind spot?
a: An area the driver cannot see
80521.e: Beside and in front of a lorry there are places the driver cannot see, even with mirrors. You are in danger there.
80521.m: In the blind spot, the lorry driver cannot see you.

80522.q: Where is it especially dangerous for cyclists next to a lorry at a junction?
a: Right beside it on the right
On the other side of the road
Far away on a cycle path
80522.e: When the lorry turns right, the driver often cannot see a bike right beside it on the right. That is why it is better to wait some distance behind.
80522.m: Never wait right beside a lorry on its right.

80523.q: What is the maximum weight of a lorry with a trailer in Switzerland?
80523.e: In Switzerland, a loaded lorry may weigh no more than 40 tonnes (as of 2025). That is about as heavy as 25 cars.
80523.m: In Switzerland, a lorry may weigh no more than 40 tonnes.

80524.q: When are large lorries in Switzerland generally not allowed to drive?
80524.e: In Switzerland there is a night-time and a Sunday driving ban for large lorries. That keeps things quieter at night and on Sundays.
80524.m: Large lorries are mostly not allowed to drive at night or on Sundays.

80525.q: What is a lorry that mixes concrete in a turning drum called?
80525.e: The drum turns while the lorry is driving. That way the concrete stays liquid until it reaches the building site.
80525.m: A cement mixer turns the concrete in a drum.

80526.q: What is a lorry that tilts its load bed to unload gravel called?
80526.e: The tipper lorry raises the front of its load bed. Then the gravel slides out at the back.
80526.m: A tipper lorry simply tips out its load.

80527.q: Which big metal boxes do lorries often carry?
80527.e: Containers are big steel boxes of standard sizes. They can be moved from ships onto trains and lorries.
80527.m: Containers are big metal boxes for goods.

80528.q: Where is a tractor mainly used?
80528.e: Farmers use the tractor for lots of jobs. It pulls machines and trailers across fields and meadows.
80528.m: The tractor is an important vehicle on the farm.

80529.q: Which wheels are bigger on many tractors?
80529.e: The big back wheels transfer the power to the ground. That way the tractor can pull heavy loads.
80529.m: Many tractors have big back wheels.

80530.q: Why do tractor tyres have deep grooves?
a: So they do not slip in the field
80530.e: The deep grooves grip the soft soil. So the wheel does not spin, even when it is wet.
80530.m: Deep grooves give the tractor grip in the field.

80531.q: What does a tractor pull across the field to turn over the soil?
80531.e: The plough cuts open the soil and turns it over. After that, the farmer can sow.
80531.m: With a plough the tractor turns over the soil.

80532.q: Which fuel do most tractors use?
80532.e: Most tractors have a diesel engine. It is powerful and well suited to heavy work.

80533.q: Why do you often have to wait behind a tractor on the road?
80533.e: Tractors are built for work, not for high speeds. So they drive slowly on the road.
80533.m: Tractors drive slowly on the road.

80534.q: What does a tractor often carry on its trailer in summer?
80534.e: In summer, grass is dried and brought in as hay. The tractor takes it to the barn.
80534.m: In summer the tractor takes hay to the barn.

80535.q: Which machine does a tractor pull to cut grass?
80535.e: The mower cuts the grass in the meadow. It becomes food for the animals.
80535.m: The tractor cuts grass with a mower.

80536.q: What do you need a digger for on a building site?
80536.e: A digger lifts out a lot of earth at once with its bucket. This makes, for example, pits for house cellars.

80537.q: What is the part at the front of the arm that the digger digs with called?
80537.e: At the front of the digger’s arm there is a bucket with teeth. With it the digger tears up the earth and lifts it.
80537.m: The digger digs with its bucket.

80538.q: Why do many big diggers move on tracks instead of wheels?
a: So they do not sink into the ground
80538.e: The wide tracks spread the great weight over a large area. So the digger sinks less into soft ground.
80538.m: Tracks stop a digger from sinking into the ground.

80539.q: What is pushed through thick hoses in a digger to move the strong arm?
80539.e: A pump pushes oil through hoses into cylinders. The oil pushes the pistons out and so moves the arm.
80539.m: A digger arm is moved by oil under pressure.

80540.q: Which special digger can climb steep slopes with its legs?
80540.e: The walking excavator has legs with wheels and can work on steep slopes and in stream beds. It was developed in the 1960s in Liechtenstein and Switzerland.
80540.m: A walking excavator climbs steep slopes with its legs.

80541.q: What is a small digger that fits even into narrow gardens called?
80541.e: A mini digger is small and light. It can get to places where a big digger has no room.
80541.m: A mini digger fits on small building sites too.

80542.q: Which huge digger digs with a big wheel full of buckets?
80542.e: On a bucket-wheel excavator, a huge wheel with lots of buckets turns. Such diggers mine coal, for example, and are among the largest vehicles in the world.
80542.m: A bucket-wheel excavator digs with a wheel full of buckets.

80543.q: What can the upper part of many diggers do?
80543.e: On many diggers, the upper part with the cab and arm can turn all the way round. That way the digger can dig and dump the earth beside it.
80543.m: The upper part of a digger can turn.

80544.q: What does a fire engine switch on in an emergency?
80544.e: With blue lights and siren, the fire brigade shows it is on its way to an emergency. Everyone else should let it pass.
80544.m: On call-outs, the fire brigade drives with blue lights and siren.

80545.q: What must cars do when a fire engine with blue lights comes?
80545.e: In an emergency every minute counts. That is why all other vehicles must make room for the fire engine.
80545.m: Make room for a fire engine with blue lights.

80546.q: What is the long ladder on a fire engine that can turn called?
80546.e: The turntable ladder can turn and extend a long way. That way the fire brigade can reach high windows and roofs.
80546.m: With the turntable ladder the fire brigade reaches high up.

80547.q: Where does the fire brigade often get water in a town?
80547.e: Hydrants are connections to the water pipes under the street. The fire brigade attaches its hoses there.
80547.m: The fire brigade gets water from a hydrant.

80548.q: What does a fire brigade water tender carry?
80548.e: A water tender has a big water tank. That way the fire brigade can start putting out a fire straight away, even where there is no hydrant.
80548.m: A water tender brings water for firefighting.

80550.q: What does a fire engine carry rolled up?
80550.e: The hoses are rolled up so they take up little space. On a call-out, the fire brigade quickly rolls them out.
80550.m: A fire engine carries long hoses.

80551.q: Why does a steep mountain railway need a cogwheel?
a: So it does not slip on the slope
80551.e: Smooth wheels slip on steep rails. A cogwheel grips a toothed rack and pulls the train up safely.
80551.m: The cogwheel stops a mountain train from slipping.

80552.q: Where is the toothed rack on a rack railway usually?
a: In the middle between the rails
Beside the track in the grass
On the roof of the train
80552.e: The rack usually lies in the middle of the track. The train’s cogwheel grips into it from above.
80552.m: The rack usually lies between the rails.

80553.q: Up which mountain did Europe’s first mountain railway run in 1871?
80553.e: In 1871 the rack railway from Vitznau up the Rigi was opened. It is considered Europe’s first mountain railway.
80553.m: Europe’s first mountain railway ran up the Rigi.

80554.q: Which Swiss engineer built rack railways such as the Rigi railway?
80554.e: Niklaus Riggenbach invented his own rack that looks like a ladder. Among other things, he used it to build the Rigi railway.
80554.m: Niklaus Riggenbach helped build the Rigi railway.

80555.q: Which rack railway on Lake Brienz still often runs with steam locomotives?
80555.e: The Brienz Rothorn Railway still mostly runs with steam locomotives today. You can see the smoke from far away.
80555.m: The Brienz Rothorn Railway still runs on steam.

80556.q: From which place does the Gornergrat Railway, with its view of the Matterhorn, depart?
80556.e: The Gornergrat Railway starts in Zermatt. At the top of the Gornergrat you have a great view of the Matterhorn.
80556.m: The Gornergrat Railway departs from Zermatt.

80557.q: What are the points around a cogwheel called?
80557.e: A cogwheel has lots of teeth all the way round. They grip into the gaps of the rack or of another cogwheel.
80557.m: A cogwheel has lots of teeth.

80558.q: How does a rack railway travel compared with a normal train?
80558.e: On a steep mountain, a rack railway travels carefully and slowly. In return, it can climb slopes that a normal train cannot manage.
80558.m: A rack railway goes slowly, but climbs steeply.

80559.q: What does the cabin of an aerial cableway hang from?
80559.e: An aerial cableway floats above the ground on steel cables. The cables are very strong and are checked regularly.
80559.m: An aerial cableway hangs from steel cables.

80560.q: Where is the motor that drives an aerial cableway usually located?
a: At the bottom of the cable
80560.e: The motor is in the valley or mountain station. It moves a cable that pulls the cabins.
80560.m: The motor of an aerial cableway is in a station.

80561.q: What is the cableway on the Titlis whose cabin rotates during the ride called?
80561.e: The Rotair on the Titlis opened in 1992 as the world’s first rotating aerial cableway. That way every passenger gets to look in all directions.
80561.m: The cabin of the Titlis Rotair rotates during the ride.

80562.q: What is special about the CabriO on the Stanserhorn?
a: You ride on the open roof
80562.e: Since 2012 the CabriO has been the world’s first aerial cableway with an open upper deck. There you stand under the open sky.
80562.m: On the CabriO you ride on an open roof.

80563.q: What are the tall structures that the cable of a cableway runs over called?
80563.e: Between the valley and the mountain there are tall steel pylons. They carry the cables so they do not sag too low.
80563.m: Tall pylons carry the cables of a cableway.

80564.q: A reversible cableway has two cabins. What do they do at the same time?
a: One goes up, one goes down
Both go round in a circle
80564.e: The two cabins hang on the same hauling cable. When one goes up, the other goes down, and they pass each other in the middle.
80564.m: On a reversible cableway, the two cabins pass each other.

80565.q: What is a cableway with lots of small cabins that keep going round called?
80565.e: On a gondola lift, lots of small cabins hang on the cable. They keep going round in a loop between the valley and the mountain.
80565.m: A gondola lift has lots of small cabins.

80566.q: Which peak near Zermatt does Europe’s highest aerial cableway lead to?
80566.e: The top station on the Klein Matterhorn is over 3,800 metres above sea level. It is the highest cableway station in Europe.
80566.m: Europe’s highest cableway station is on the Klein Matterhorn.

80567.q: What do you sit on in a chairlift?
80567.e: On a chairlift, open seats hang from the cable. You float up the mountain in the open air.
80567.m: On a chairlift you sit on an open seat on the cable.

80568.q: What must be closed after you sit down on a chairlift?
80568.e: The safety bar is folded down in front of your body. It stops you from sliding out of the chair.
80568.m: On a chairlift you close the safety bar.

80569.q: What protects you from wind and snow on some chairlifts?
80569.e: Some chairlifts have a see-through bubble. You pull it down over the seat like a bell.
80569.m: A bubble protects you from wind and snow on a chairlift.

80570.q: What should you not do on a chairlift?
80570.e: Swinging is dangerous and can disrupt the whole lift. You sit still until you reach the top.
80570.m: On a chairlift you sit still and do not swing.

80571.q: What do some chairlifts have so you do not get cold in winter?
80571.e: Many modern chairlifts have heated seats. The chairs are warmed up in the station.

80572.q: What do you do when you arrive at the top on a chairlift?
a: Open the bar and stand up
80572.e: Shortly before the station you open the bar. At the exit point you stand up and ski or walk away quickly.
80572.m: At the top, open the bar and get off quickly.

80573.q: What is different about a chairlift compared with a gondola lift?
a: You sit in the open air
80573.e: On a gondola lift you sit in a closed cabin. On a chairlift you sit outside in the fresh air.
80573.m: On a chairlift you sit in the open air.

80574.q: Who often rides a chairlift in summer?
80574.e: Many chairlifts also run in summer. Then they take hikers comfortably up the mountain.
80574.m: In summer, hikers ride the chairlift.

80576.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the Rega air rescue service?
80576.e: Rega’s emergency number is 1414. It sends rescue helicopters to injured people, for example in the mountains.

80577.q: Why does a helicopter have a small rotor at the back?
a: So it does not spin round in a circle
80577.e: The big rotor turns and would make the helicopter turn with it. The small tail rotor works against this.
80577.m: The small tail rotor keeps the helicopter straight.

80578.q: What can a helicopter do that a normal plane cannot?
80578.e: A helicopter can hover in one place in the air. That is why it can rescue people even on steep rock faces.
80578.m: A helicopter can stay still in the air.

80579.q: What does a helicopter not need to take off?
80579.e: A helicopter takes off straight upwards. That is why it can land and take off even in a small meadow.
80579.m: A helicopter does not need a long runway.

80580.q: Who built one of the first really usable helicopters in 1939?
80580.e: In 1939 Igor Sikorsky built the VS-300 in the USA. It is seen as the model for many later helicopters.
80580.m: Igor Sikorsky built an early helicopter in 1939.

80581.q: What do helicopters in the Alps often bring to mountain huts?
80581.e: Many mountain huts have no road leading to them. That is why helicopters bring food, drinks and building materials up to them.

80582.q: Which letter is often painted large on a helicopter landing pad?
80582.e: The big H shows pilots from the air where they are allowed to land. You find it, for example, on hospital roofs.
80582.m: A big H marks a helicopter landing pad.

80583.q: Where does a rescue helicopter land at many hospitals?
80583.e: Many hospitals have a landing pad on the roof. From there, injured people get quickly to A&E by lift.
80583.m: Rescue helicopters often land on the hospital roof.

80585.q: Which colour is at the very top of a traffic light for cars?
80585.e: Red is at the top, amber in the middle and green at the bottom. That way even colour-blind people can tell from the position which light is on.
80585.m: On a traffic light, red is at the very top.

80586.q: What does a red traffic light mean?
80586.e: At red you must stop in front of the traffic light. Only at green may you drive on.

80587.q: What does amber mean on a traffic light for cars?
a: Stop if you still safely can
80587.e: Amber shows that red is about to come. Anyone who can still stop safely must stop.
80587.m: At amber you stop if you still safely can.

80588.q: In which city was the world’s first traffic light set up in 1868?
80588.e: The first traffic light was set up in London in 1868. It was lit by gas and operated by a policeman.
80588.m: The first traffic light was in London.

80589.q: What do pedestrians press at some traffic lights?
80589.e: With the button you tell the traffic light that you want to cross the road. Then it soon switches to green.
80589.m: You press the button to signal at the traffic light.

80590.q: How does a traffic light help blind people?
80590.e: Many traffic lights have a button that vibrates at green, or they make sounds. That way blind people know when they may cross.
80590.m: Some traffic lights tick or vibrate for blind people.

80591.q: What does the green pedestrian light show?
80591.e: On a pedestrian light, a walking figure lights up at green. At red the figure stands still.
80591.m: At green, the pedestrian light shows a walking figure.

80592.q: What does a flashing amber traffic light mean?
80592.e: A flashing amber light warns of a danger, for example when the traffic light is switched off. You then drive especially carefully.
80592.m: A flashing amber light calls for care.

80594.q: What colour are zebra crossings in Switzerland?
80594.e: In Switzerland, zebra crossings are yellow. In many other countries, for example in Germany, they are white.
80594.m: In Switzerland, zebra crossings are yellow.

80595.q: How do you cross a zebra crossing correctly?
a: Run as fast as you can
Stop in the middle of it
80595.e: If you run, you can trip or be seen too late. That is why you walk briskly across the road.
80595.m: Cross a zebra crossing briskly without running.

80596.q: What is the best way to tell whether a driver has seen you?
80596.e: If you look the driver in the eye, you can tell whether they have noticed you. Only when the car has stopped do you start walking.
80596.m: Eye contact tells you whether the driver has seen you.

80597.q: In Switzerland, who has right of way at a zebra crossing?
a: Pedestrians who want to cross the road
80597.e: Cars must stop when someone at the zebra crossing clearly wants to cross the road. Even so, you always check first whether the cars really stop.
80597.m: At a zebra crossing, pedestrians have right of way.

80598.q: Who has right of way over cars at a zebra crossing?
80598.e: Cars must stop when someone is on the zebra crossing or clearly wants to cross. Even so, you always check whether the car really stops.
80598.m: At a zebra crossing, pedestrians have right of way over cars.

80599.q: Where is the safest place to cross a road?
80599.e: At a zebra crossing, drivers expect pedestrians. Between cars or on bends, people cannot see each other well.
80599.m: The safest place to cross the road is the zebra crossing.

80600.q: What did pedestrians in Switzerland have to do at a zebra crossing until 1994?
80600.e: Until 1994 you had to show with your hand that you wanted to cross the road. This rule was then abolished.
80600.m: Until 1994 you gave a hand signal at a zebra crossing.

80601.q: The PostBus leaves at 8.10 and arrives in the village at 8.30. How long does the journey take?
80601.m: The journey time is the time between departure and arrival.

80602.q: A train runs every half hour. One leaves at 9.00. When does the next one leave?
80602.e: Half an hour has 30 minutes. 9.00 plus 30 minutes is 9.30.

80603.q: The timetable says 14.00. What time is that in the afternoon?
80603.e: After 12 o’clock you keep counting: 13, 14 and so on. 14 − 12 = 2, so it is 2 o’clock in the afternoon.
80603.m: Timetables count the hours up to 24.

80604.q: The tram runs every 10 minutes. One leaves at 7.20. When does the next one leave?
80604.m: With a regular timetable, the trams always run at the same interval.

80605.q: You are at the bus stop at 10.05. The next bus leaves at 10.20. How long do you wait?
80605.m: You work out the waiting time from now until departure.

80606.q: A train leaves at 17.50. The journey takes 20 minutes. When does it arrive?
80606.e: It is 10 minutes until 18.00, then another 10 minutes. So the train arrives at 18.10.
80606.m: After 59 minutes a new hour begins.

80607.q: What is the place called where a bus or tram stops so that you can get on?
80607.e: The bus or tram stops at the stop. The timetable often hangs there too.
80607.m: You get on the bus at the bus stop.

80608.q: Which departure in the timetable is the earliest?
80608.e: 6 o’clock comes before 7 and 8 o’clock. So 6.45 is the earliest departure.
